primary_sources: Punch, “The Child Who Wanted to Play by Himself,” December 1919

stimulus.source_note: Punch (London), “The Child Who Wanted to Play by Himself,” December 1919, public domain.
stimulus.text: A December 1919 cartoon in Punch, a London magazine, titled “The Child Who Wanted to Play by Himself,” shows President Woodrow Wilson pulling a small child wearing a hat marked “U.S.A.” toward a building labeled “Temple of Peace,” where other children play inside. Wilson says, “Now come along and enjoy yourself with the other children. I promised that you’d be the life and soul of the party.”

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Punch (London), “The Child Who Wanted to Play by Himself,” December 1919, public domain.
stem: Which of the following best explains why Wilson is shown doing the persuading, rather than the child acting on its own?

options.text: Wilson had already won Senate approval for the League, and the cartoon celebrates his victory.
options.misconception: The Senate never approved the treaty, so there was no victory to celebrate.

options.text: The cartoonist believed the American people had demanded the League and Wilson was merely carrying out their wishes.
options.misconception: The child resists in the drawing; the cartoon shows reluctance, not a popular demand.

options.text: Wilson wanted the United States to annex the defeated Central Powers as colonies.
options.misconception: Wilson’s Fourteen Points called for self-determination, the opposite of annexing defeated peoples.

options.text: Wilson had staked his peace plan on the League, but the Senate and public would not accept its obligations.

figures.caption: Punch, “The Child Who Wanted to Play by Himself,” December 1919
figures.alt: A 1919 Punch cartoon shows President Wilson pulling a small child in a U.S.A. hat toward a building labeled Temple of Peace

rationales.A: The Senate never approved the treaty. There was no victory for the cartoon to celebrate.
rationales.B: The child resists in the drawing. The cartoon shows reluctance, not a popular demand for the League.
rationales.C: Wilson’s Fourteen Points called for self-determination. Annexing defeated peoples is the opposite of what he proposed.
rationales.D: The joke is the gap between Wilson’s promise, that America would be “the life and soul of the party,” and a country pulling away. Background: Article 10 of the League Covenant, the pledge of collective security, was at the center of the Senate’s reservations fight.
rationales.general:
1. Look at who is active. Wilson pulls and promises; the child only resists.
2. Ask what Wilson promised. He told the Allies that America would lead the League and keep the peace.
3. Ask who had to agree. The Senate had to approve the treaty, and many senators feared the League would drag America into foreign wars.
4. Put it together. The persuasion is Wilson’s because the commitment was his before it was the country’s.
Remember: when a leader is shown dragging a country somewhere, ask who has to say yes before the country can move.
